sections.title: High performance
sections.subtitle: so your customers don't have to wait.
paragraphs: At Atomic Concept, we design application architecture around the needs of each project. Event-driven patterns can help separate responsibilities and track changes. Performance depends on the complete system, from the interface to server operations and data storage.

sections.title: Easy and understandable project maintenance
sections.subtitle: if you want to outsource the code to another development team in the future.
paragraphs: The structure of the source code will remain clear and documented where needed. This gives your team visibility and makes future improvements easier, including a handover to another development team.

sections.title: High scalability through modularization
sections.subtitle: in case of rapid growth of your business.
paragraphs: A modular application has clear boundaries between its parts. Domain-Driven Design and separating changes from queries (CQRS) can help establish those boundaries when the project needs them. If a particular operation becomes heavily used, we can consider scaling that part independently.

Modular frontend code helps us control what the browser needs to load. On the backend, separate modules can make changes and deployment easier. These choices support performance work, but do not guarantee a particular speed or score.
Where it makes sense, components can be reused in other parts of the application or in another project.

sections.title: Time is always flowing
sections.subtitle: let's not forget that.
paragraphs: When designing connected systems, we consider **what happened and when**. An event records a particular change at a particular time. An appropriate event history can help reconstruct the sequence of operations when investigating a claim or a missing record.

sections.title: Lightning fast User Interface
sections.subtitle: to help your client feel the flow.
paragraphs: **A good application is one that helps the user.** Well-written, optimised code makes good use of modern browsers.

We do not make the user wait where it is unnecessary. When waiting is unavoidable, for example during a database operation, the interface should explain what is happening. Loading indicators and carefully chosen transitions can help the experience remain clear.

sections.title: Comfort in any situation
sections.subtitle: because real life is not perfect.
paragraphs: Sometimes the internet connection drops. A failed request should not mean losing all the work a person has just done.

Depending on the application, we can preserve a form draft, show a clear connection warning or queue suitable operations until the connection returns. The architecture needs to support the way people actually use the service.

sections.title: Good communication is key
sections.subtitle: to get full speed.
paragraphs: A good frontend alone is not enough. Interface behaviour, server operations and database models need consistent requirements. Sending only the information needed for a particular task also avoids unnecessary network traffic.
At Atomic Concept, we design around business processes, using approaches such as Domain-Driven Design where useful. **Technology is a tool, not a toy.**

sections.title: Backend that fits the application
sections.subtitle: without unnecessary overhead.
paragraphs: The backend must work closely with the user interface. At every stage of server development, we focus on the operations your business needs and the information your customers need to use them.
We avoid unnecessary data transfer and server work. We consider performance and the ability to handle growth when planning the system.

sections.title: We don't promise miracles at the beginning
sections.subtitle: we spend more time analyzing.
paragraphs: **The best job done is the one that accomplishes your needs without overcomplicated solutions.**
The key to success is analysis. We need to understand exactly what you want to achieve. Then we can build a service with a clear purpose, without unnecessary complexity.
Things that are too complicated and hard to understand can seem professional at first glance. Over time, they become expensive to maintain.

sections.title: Digital solutions in an analog world
sections.subtitle: it's not that difficult.
paragraphs: Many things that seem abstract have equivalents in the real world. We can find those connections and explain them in the context of your business. That makes it easier to plan an application together and understand how it works.

sections.title: Start with the work you want to improve
sections.subtitle: You do not need to choose the technology.
paragraphs: Tell us what you do today, which tools you use and where you need help. We will check whether an existing product is enough or whether you need something built for your business.
**We don't promise miracles at the beginning.** We spend more time analysing. The best job done is the one that accomplishes your needs without overcomplicated solutions.

sections.title: One useful first step
sections.subtitle: Then decide what comes next.
paragraphs: We agree the scope, the way to check the result and the cost of running the solution before implementation. You can start with one process, one integration or one part of an application.
After implementation, we test it with your team and prepare the handover. Further development and maintenance can be agreed around what you actually need.

sections.title: Michał Sałek, the person behind Atomic Concept
sections.subtitle: From understanding the problem to running the application.
paragraphs: I have worked professionally in software development since 2019. I build complete applications, connect external services and integrate AI. I also take care of deployment and maintenance.

You discuss the project directly with the person who builds it. I work remotely from Kraków with clients in Poland and abroad. You can see my [public engineering work](https://github.com/MichalSalek).

sections.title: Which repeated task would you like to stop doing by hand?
sections.subtitle: Start with a specific piece of work.
paragraphs: Examples include reading information from documents, sorting incoming enquiries, preparing a draft response or finding an answer in company materials. We can connect those steps to the tools your team already uses.

A fixed rule or a ready-made integration may be enough. AI is useful when the task involves interpreting text, recognising information or working with material that does not always follow the same format.

sections.title: Your documents and systems
sections.subtitle: A useful result in the place where you work.
paragraphs: An automation can take information from an email or form, check what is missing and prepare a record in your customer system. A search tool can find relevant passages in the documents you allow it to use.
These are examples of possible implementations. The choice depends on your data, access to the existing systems and the quality you need. We agree what to do when information is missing or uncertain.

sections.title: AI prepares. You decide what needs approval.
sections.subtitle: Check the result before taking an important action.
paragraphs: For a customer reply, a quote or a change to business data, we can prepare a draft for a person to approve. We define which tasks may run automatically and where your team should make the final decision.
We test on representative examples, check mistakes and estimate the ongoing cost. We also agree which data may be sent to an external AI provider and what should remain inside your systems.

sections.title: A working process, with a clear handover
sections.subtitle: Implementation is more than access to a model.
paragraphs: The work can include mapping the process, connecting services, testing outputs, recording failures and showing your team how to use the solution. Monitoring and ongoing support are scoped to the implementation.
Describe one repeated task in the contact form. Tell us how you do it now and what you would like to happen instead.
For more engineering background, read about [planning and maintaining an application](/software/architecture/).

sections.title: Let your existing tools exchange information
sections.subtitle: Without copying the same data again.
paragraphs: A website form can create an enquiry in your customer system. A shop can pass order and payment information to another service. A completed task can update a report or notify the person responsible.
We first check which connections the existing products support. Where their built-in features are enough, we use them. A custom integration fills the part that is missing.

sections.title: Which data should be shared?
sections.subtitle: Agree a source of truth for each record.
paragraphs: We decide where an order or customer record originates and which tools should receive a copy. We also agree where changes are made and how to match corresponding records.

Copying data alone is not always enough. We map fields and handle missing information. Useful [reports](/software/reporting/) or [workflow automation](/software/automation/) can be added around that connection.

sections.title: When a connection fails
sections.subtitle: The missing record should not disappear quietly.
paragraphs: External systems sometimes time out or send the same information twice. We account for retries, duplicate records and errors when designing the integration.

Depending on the scope, we can keep a history of changes, flag records that need attention and provide a way to resume work after a failure. Your team should know what succeeded and what still needs checking.

sections.title: Build on what already works
sections.subtitle: An integration does not have to replace your system.
paragraphs: We can add one missing connection to an existing application or gradually improve a larger flow. Access, available interfaces and the condition of the current software determine what is possible.
Tell us which programs you use and where you currently re-enter or reconcile information. We will use that as the starting point.
For more engineering background, read about [server operations and data processing](/software/backend/).

sections.title: An application built around the way you work
sections.subtitle: Tasks for customers and your team in one system.
paragraphs: You may need a customer portal, a booking flow, a job management tool or an employee panel. An application stores records, tracks their status and makes them available to the appropriate people.

The first step is understanding the task. We check whether an existing product can do the job before recommending a custom system. If you mainly need to present an offer and receive enquiries, see [business websites](/software/websites/).

sections.title: Take care of the whole application
sections.subtitle: From the screen to the information behind it.
paragraphs: A usable interface, stored data, access permissions, payments and external services need to work together. Atomic Concept can handle those parts as one project, including testing and deployment.
We also work on existing software. A new feature, an integration or a performance improvement may be a better next step than starting again.

sections.title: Fast and comfortable to use
sections.subtitle: Because real life is not perfect.
paragraphs: A good application is one that helps the user. We pay attention to mobile screens, loading time, clear feedback and what happens when a request fails.
A customer should not have to guess whether a form was sent or lose everything after an unsuccessful attempt. We include those situations in the design and testing of the agreed features.

sections.title: Easy and understandable project maintenance
sections.subtitle: Leave room for the next change.
paragraphs: We keep the structure of the source code clear and document the parts needed to run and develop the application. That also helps if you choose another development team in the future.
We agree the handover, hosting and support arrangements as part of the project. Start by describing who will use the solution and what they need to accomplish.
For more engineering background, read about [the user interface](/software/frontend/).

sections.title: What should a customer find on your website?
sections.subtitle: An offer they can understand and easily ask about.
paragraphs: A business website can explain your services, show selected work and make contact straightforward. We start by asking why a person would visit and what they should be able to do next.
We organise pages and content around those questions. For example, a service business might need separate service descriptions, its coverage area, selected work and an enquiry form.

sections.title: Clear on a phone and a computer
sections.subtitle: Without unnecessary waiting or a shifting layout.
paragraphs: We pay attention to loading speed, readable text and reserved space for images. Forms and navigation are checked on small screens as well as desktop.
If you need several languages, we prepare distinct URLs and complete content for each version. A site can remain static when you do not need server-dependent features.

sections.title: Content that search and AI systems can read
sections.subtitle: Start with a clear offer and sound technical foundations.
paragraphs: We prepare titles, descriptions, structured data, links between pages and a sitemap. Important information should also be available without running scripts.

These measures make the content easier to read and understand. They do not guarantee a Google position or a recommendation from an AI model. Real work examples and useful answers for customers still matter.

sections.title: Deployment and future changes
sections.subtitle: Keep the parts you already have.
paragraphs: We can use your existing domain, email and hosting, or agree a new publishing setup. We also decide who will update the content and how they will do it.

If you need customer accounts or job management as well as an offer website, see [applications and systems](/software/custom-software/). A form can also [connect to your existing customer system](/software/integrations/).

sections.title: Which task do you repeat every day?
sections.subtitle: Map what starts the work and what should happen next.
paragraphs: A new enquiry can create a task for the right person, receive a reference number and trigger an acknowledgement. An approaching deadline can prompt a reminder, while completed work can update an order status.
These are examples of possible workflows. We first examine how your team works and choose one useful part to improve.

sections.title: Clear rules for the next step
sections.subtitle: Each step has a condition and an expected result.
paragraphs: We agree where an enquiry comes from, which information is required, who should receive the task and what happens when something is missing. The process can include approval by a person.

Not every automation needs AI. When a fixed rule is enough, a simpler solution can be easier to verify and maintain. [AI](/software/ai-automation/) can help with tasks that require interpreting free text.

sections.title: Plan for exceptions too
sections.subtitle: Missing data or a failed connection should not stop work silently.
paragraphs: We consider duplicate enquiries, unavailable systems and missed deadlines. Depending on the task, an operation can be retried or passed to a person to check.
We agree who should see an error and how to resume the process. Your team should know which tasks completed and which still need attention.

sections.title: Start with one process
sections.subtitle: Expand after checking it works.
paragraphs: Before implementation, we agree the scope, running cost and way to check the result. We use built-in product features where they are enough for the task.
Describe the steps you follow and the tools between which you move information. If you only need data exchange, see [system integrations](/software/integrations/).

sections.title: Which information do you need to run the business?
sections.subtitle: Choose the question before the chart.
paragraphs: How many orders are waiting? Which payments are overdue? How are sales distributed across services? These are the kinds of questions we use to plan a report.
We choose the information you actually use. The result might be a recurring email, a spreadsheet or a dashboard in your browser.

sections.title: One report from several sources
sections.subtitle: Without assembling the same data by hand each time.
paragraphs: We can bring together information from your shop, payments, customer system or spreadsheets. First we check data access and how to match records about the same customer or job.
Where a connection is missing, we can build an [integration](/software/integrations/). You do not have to replace the tools your team uses to start reporting.

sections.title: Know where the number came from
sections.subtitle: And when it was last updated.
paragraphs: We agree what each measure means, its source and the update frequency. A report should clearly show the period it covers and whether all information was retrieved.
Incomplete or outdated information needs to be marked. Before deployment, we compare the results with the sources and check cases that could distort the summary.

sections.title: Information for the people who need it
sections.subtitle: With an appropriate level of access.
paragraphs: An owner may need a company-wide summary while an employee needs their own jobs. If we build a dashboard, we also agree how people sign in and what they may see.
Tell us which report you prepare by hand and which decision it supports. If you also need to record jobs and manage the work itself, see [applications and systems](/software/custom-software/).
